expectedText:
REAL ESTATE TRANSFER DISCLOSURE STATEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA · Jane Doe

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law on the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement, Civil Code section 1102 et seq. (Article 1.5 of Chapter 2 of Title 4 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Civil Code, sections 1102 through 1102.19), as it may relate to the transfer of the real property at 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA, where Jane Doe is named as seller and John Smith is named as buyer. It states what California law provides about which transfers this disclosure article covers, the statute's own list of exempt transfers, the statutory disclosure form and the underlying duty to disclose material facts, when the completed disclosure statement must be delivered, the buyer's statutory right to terminate an offer after a late or amended disclosure, and the stated consequence of noncompliance. It is separate from, and in addition to, any Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement, Mello-Roos special tax notice, smoke alarm/carbon monoxide compliance statement, HOA/CC&R disclosure, lead-based paint disclosure, or Megan's Law database notice provided in connection with this transaction, each of which is a distinct disclosure obligation under separate statutory provisions. This information sheet is not itself the statutory Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement that Civil Code section 1102.6 requires, and it does not tell Jane Doe, John Smith, or any real estate agent involved whether this specific transaction is covered, which exemption (if any) applies, or how to proceed.

WHICH TRANSFERS THIS DISCLOSURE LAW COVERS
California's transfer disclosure statute applies to any transfer of single-family residential property by sale, exchange, real property sales contract, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, except as separately provided by the statute's own list of exemptions. The statute borrows certain definitions used elsewhere in real estate licensing law for purposes of this article. Any waiver of the article's requirements is void as against public policy — a seller and buyer cannot agree around this disclosure requirement by contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(a), California Civil Code, scope of the transfer disclosure statement requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.)
  "For purposes of this article, the definitions contained in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code shall apply."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(b), California Civil Code, cross-reference to real estate licensing definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.)
  "Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(c), California Civil Code, waiver of the disclosure requirement is void (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.)
  Known gap: The statute's own scope term is "single-family residential property" — this article does not itself define that term by a numeric unit count (e.g., "one to four dwelling units"), and this clause does not equate it with the differently-worded "one to four dwelling units" scope language that a separate California disclosure statute (the Megan's Law database notice, cited elsewhere in this corpus) uses; a specific property's classification under either phrase is not resolved here. Subdivision (b)'s cross-reference is to the definitions chapter of the Business and Professions Code real estate license law (commencing at Section 10000), which is a body of licensing definitions, not a further definition of "single-family residential property" itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines the scope of its residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; disclosure scope and terminology vary by state. All three citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1102); none is an independent source for another.

STATUTORY EXEMPTIONS FROM THE DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENT
The statute lists specific categories of transfers to which this disclosure article does not apply. These include: sales or transfers preceded by a subdivision public report, or made under the exception to that public-report requirement; sales or transfers made pursuant to court order, including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, foreclosure sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent-domain sales, and decree-of-specific-performance sales; a separately stated category of sales or transfers to a mortgagee, deed-of-trust beneficiary, or their successor arising out of a default and a foreclosure-type sale (including sales of a manufactured home or mobilehome by reason of default or foreclosure of a security interest); sales or transfers by a fiduciary administering a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate, subject to its own exception where the trustee is a natural person who is also a former owner or recent occupant of the property; transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the transferor's line of consanguinity; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation judgment or an incidental property settlement agreement; sales or transfers by the Controller administering unclaimed property under the Code of Civil Procedure; sales or transfers under specified Revenue and Taxation Code tax-sale provisions; sales, transfers, or exchanges to or from a governmental entity; transfers of a portion of a property that does not itself constitute single-family residential property; and the sale, creation, or transfer of a lease of any duration, other than a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with improvements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Sales or transfers that are required to be preceded by the furnishing to a prospective buyer of a copy of a public report pursuant to Section 11018.1 of the Business and Professions Code and transfers that can be made without a public report pursuant to Section 11010.4 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(a), California Civil Code, subdivision public report exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers pursuant to court order, including, but not limited to, sales ordered by a probate court in the administration of an estate, sales pursuant to a writ of execution, sales by any foreclosure sale, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, sales by eminent domain, and sales resulting from a decree for specific performance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(b), California Civil Code, court-order/foreclosure/bankruptcy exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers to a mortgagee by a mortgagor or successor in interest who is in default, sales to a beneficiary of a deed of trust by a trustor or successor in interest who is in default, any foreclosure sale after default, any foreclosure sale after default in an obligation secured by a mortgage, a sale under a power of sale or any foreclosure sale under a decree of foreclosure after default in an obligation secured by a deed of trust or secured by any other instrument containing a power of sale, sales by a mortgagee or a beneficiary under a deed of trust who has acquired the real property at a sale conducted pursuant to a power of sale under a mortgage or deed of trust or a sale pursuant to a decree of foreclosure or has acquired the real property by a deed in lieu of foreclosure, sales to the legal owner or lienholder of a manufactured home or mobilehome by a registered owner or successor in interest who is in default, or sales by reason of any foreclosure of a security interest in a manufactured home or mobilehome."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(c), California Civil Code, mortgagee/beneficiary default and foreclosure-sale exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers by a fiduciary in the course of the administration of a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent’s estate. This exemption shall not apply to a sale if the trustee is a natural person who is a trustee of a revocable trust and is a former owner of the property or was an occupant in possession of the property within the preceding year."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(d), California Civil Code, fiduciary/estate-administration exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers from one coowner to one or more other coowners."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(e), California Civil Code, co-owner-to-co-owner exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers made to a spouse, or to a person or persons in the line of consanguinity of one or more of the transferors."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(f), California Civil Code, spouse/direct-relative exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers between spouses resulting from a judgment of dissolution of marriage or of legal separation or from a property settlement agreement incidental to that judgment."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(g), California Civil Code, divorce/legal-separation exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers by the Controller in the course of administering Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 1500) of Title 10 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(h), California Civil Code, Controller/unclaimed-property administration exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 3691) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3771) of Part 6 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(i), California Civil Code, tax-sale exemption under the Revenue and Taxation Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers or exchanges to or from any governmental entity."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(j), California Civil Code, governmental-entity exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "Sales or transfers of any portion of a property not constituting single-family residential property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(k), California Civil Code, partial-property/not-single-family exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  "The sale, creation, or transfer of any lease of any duration with the exception of a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with improvements."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(l), California Civil Code, lease-without-purchase-option exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.2.)
  Known gap: This is a longer and more specific exemption list than commonly assumed — twelve separate lettered categories in the statute as currently in force, not only the handful most often cited (court order, fiduciary, co-owner, spouse, divorce-related, and governmental-entity transfers). This corpus's Residential Purchase Agreement document already cites six of these same lettered exemptions (subdivisions (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), and (j)) in an embedded clause covering the transfer disclosure statement generally; this clause independently verifies those six and adds citations to six further exemption categories from the same statutory section — subdivisions (a), (c), (h), (i), (k), and (l) — that are not otherwise cited elsewhere in this corpus. All twelve citations below are subdivisions of one statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.2); none is an independent source for another. A thirteenth subdivision of the same section, not quoted here, states an interpretive rule about the meaning of "sale" and "transfer" and a savings clause for a 2018 amendment — it is not itself an exemption category. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines its exemptions from a residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer, and it does not determine whether any specific transfer actually falls within any of these categories.

THE STATUTORY DISCLOSURE FORM AND THE UNDERLYING DUTY TO DISCLOSE
The disclosures this article requires must be made on a copy of a specific statutory disclosure form. Separately, the Legislature has stated that this article does not affect the existing obligation of the parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property — including the property's physical conditions and previously received reports of physical inspections — and that this article does not change a real estate broker's or salesperson's separate statutory duty of disclosure. The Legislature has also stated its intent that delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an "as is" sale, citing a 1993 California Court of Appeal decision on that point.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The disclosures required by this article pertaining to the property proposed to be transferred are set forth in, and shall be made on a copy of, the following disclosure form:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6(a), California Civil Code, the disclosure must be made on the statutory form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.6.)
  "The Legislature did not intend to affect the existing obligations of the parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including, but not limited to, the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections noted on the disclosure form set forth in Section 1102.6 or 1102.6a, and that nothing in this article shall be construed to change the duty of a real estate broker or salesperson pursuant to Section 2079."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.1(a), California Civil Code, the underlying material-fact disclosure duty is preserved (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.1.)
  "It is also the intent of the Legislature that the delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an “as is” sale, as held in Loughrin v. Superior Court (1993) 15 Cal. App. 4th 1188."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.1(a) [as-is sale], California Civil Code, disclosure cannot be waived in an 'as is' sale (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.1.)
  Known gap: The exact, current checkbox-by-checkbox wording of the statutory disclosure form itself (Civil Code § 1102.6) could not be confirmed from a fetchable primary source, re-verified independently on 2026-09-05: leginfo's own page for § 1102.6 displays a literal "NOTICE OF INCOMPLETE TEXT" placeholder rather than the form's actual content, stating that the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement instead appears in the published bill (Sec. 25, Chapter 370, Statutes of 2020, pages 34-38) rather than on the statute page itself. Because of that, this clause does not quote the form's specific line items (named systems, appliances, or specific defect/environmental/legal categories) as statutory language — doing so would have meant asserting text that could not be independently verified from the fetched leginfo source. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a residential transfer-disclosure obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer. The two quotes below credited to § 1102.1(a) are from a single statutory subdivision, itself independent from § 1102.6(a); no additional independent source was located for either § 1102.1(a) point.

WHEN THE DISCLOSURE STATEMENT MUST BE DELIVERED
The statute sets separate delivery deadlines depending on the type of transfer. In the case of a sale, the seller must deliver the completed disclosure statement to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable before transfer of title. In the case of a sale by a real property sales contract, a lease together with an option to purchase, or a ground lease coupled with improvements, the seller must instead deliver it as soon as practicable before execution of the contract — with "execution" meaning, for this purpose, the making or acceptance of an offer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "In the case of a sale, as soon as practicable before transfer of title."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3(a), California Civil Code, delivery timing for a sale — as soon as practicable before transfer of title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.3.)
  "In the case of sale by a real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985, or by a lease together with an option to purchase, or a ground lease coupled with improvements, as soon as practicable before execution of the contract."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3(b), California Civil Code, delivery timing for a real property sales contract or lease-option (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.3.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's disclosure-timing rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; timing rules vary by state. The two citations below are separate lettered subdivisions ((a) and (b)) of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.3); the buyer's right to terminate after a late-delivered disclosure is addressed in a separate clause, drawn from a third subdivision ((c)) of this same section.

BUYER'S RIGHT TO TERMINATE AFTER A LATE OR AMENDED DISCLOSURE
If any disclosure, or any material amendment of a disclosure, required by this article is delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase has already been executed, the statute gives the prospective buyer a fixed period to terminate that offer by delivering written notice of termination to the seller or the seller's agent: three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction electronically under the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. Separately, the statute specifies when this notice-and-termination period begins to run for the disclosure statement as a whole: it commences when Sections I and II of the statutory form — and, if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction, Section III as well — are completed and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's agent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "If any disclosure, or any material amendment of any disclosure, required to be made by this article, is delivered after the execution of an offer to purchase, the prospective buyer shall have three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record in transactions where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction by electronic means, pursuant to provisions of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (Title 2.5 (commencing with Section 1633.1) of Part 2 of Division 3), to terminate the offer by delivery of a written notice of termination to the seller or the seller’s agent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3(c), California Civil Code, the 3/5/5-day termination right for a late-delivered disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.3.)
  "The period of time the prospective buyer has in which to terminate the offer commences when Sections I and II, and, if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction, then also Section III, in the form described in Section 1102.6, are completed and delivered to the buyer or buyer’s agent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3(c) [trigger for the disclosure statement as a whole], California Civil Code, when the completion/delivery clock starts for Sections I, II, and III (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.3.)
  Known gap: This termination right is triggered specifically by a disclosure or material amendment delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase was already executed; the statute's own text does not, by its terms, create a freestanding right to cancel at some later time based solely on having received a disclosure that was delivered before the offer was signed. The statute's own term for this right is to "terminate the offer" by written notice — not "rescind" the contract — though this right is sometimes informally described using rescission-type language; that informal shorthand is not the statute's own wording. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's late-disclosure cure mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; termination windows and triggering events vary by state. Both citations below are the same lettered subdivision ((c)) of Civil Code § 1102.3; the separate, independent consequence of a seller's or agent's noncompliance with this article generally (as opposed to this specific termination right) is addressed in another clause, citing Civil Code § 1102.13.

EFFECT OF NONCOMPLIANCE
The statute specifies a particular consequence for noncompliance with this disclosure article. No transfer subject to the article is invalidated solely because of a failure to comply with any of its provisions. However, any person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty this article prescribes is liable to a transferee for the transferee's actual damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "No transfer subject to this article shall be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with any provision of this article. However, any person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty prescribed by any provision of this article shall be liable in the amount of actual damages suffered by a transferee."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.13, California Civil Code, noncompliance does not invalidate the transfer, but creates liability for actual damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1102.13.)
  Known gap: This is a single, independent statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.13), not a subdivision of a section quoted elsewhere in this document. The statute's own text does not define "willfully," "negligently," or "actual damages" for this purpose, and this clause does not resolve whether any specific act or omission meets that standard, or what a transferee's actual damages would be in any given case. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's remedy for noncompliance with its residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; remedies for disclosure noncompliance vary by state.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT AND REVIEW
By signing below, the undersigned acknowledge that they have received and reviewed this information sheet describing California's Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement requirement, Civil Code section 1102 et seq., in connection with the property at 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA. This information sheet is not the statutory Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement required by Civil Code section 1102.6, does not itself disclose any fact about 123 Main St., Los Angeles, CA, and does not satisfy any disclosure, exemption-determination, timing, or termination-notice obligation that the statute separately requires.

Seller: Jane Doe
Signature: _______________________  Date: January 1, 2026

Seller's Agent (if any): Alex Realtor
Signature: _______________________  Date: January 1, 2026

Buyer: John Smith
Signature: _______________________  Date: January 1, 2026

Executed at Los Angeles, California.

expectedJSON.body: The disclosures this article requires must be made on a copy of a specific statutory disclosure form. Separately, the Legislature has stated that this article does not affect the existing obligation of the parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property — including the property's physical conditions and previously received reports of physical inspections — and that this article does not change a real estate broker's or salesperson's separate statutory duty of disclosure. The Legislature has also stated its intent that delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an "as is" sale, citing a 1993 California Court of Appeal decision on that point.

Separately, the statute specifies when this notice-and-termination period begins to run for the disclosure statement as a whole: it commences when Sections I and II of the statutory form — and, if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction, Section III as well — are completed and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's agent.

No transfer subject to the article is invalidated solely because of a failure to comply with any of its provisions.
